vulnerabilities.title: Apache HTTP Server HTTP/2 Pre-Auth Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-119618, CVSS 9.8) - Fix Released 11 November, Reliable Exploit Demonstrated, Debian/Amazon Linux Packages Still Lagging
affected_products: Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 (only with HTTP/2 enabled)
Standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42
Downstream distribution packages: Debian bookworm/trixie/forky (fix pending per secondary reporting), Amazon Linux (pending), RHEL 9/10 (fixed)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - cross-cutting, highest practical exposure in this window. Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 was released on 11 November 2026 to fix CVE-2026-119618, a race condition in the mod_http2 module that corrupts heap memory and, per multiple write-ups (Wiz, The Hacker News, securityonline.info), permits unauthenticated remote code execution. Reported CVSS is 9.8. Affected builds are 2.4.55 to 2.4.70 and standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 to 2.0.42, but ONLY where HTTP/2 is enabled - that is, where the Protocols directive includes h2 or h2c. This matters disproportionately to the UK public sector: Apache remains the default front door for a large share of GOV.UK-adjacent services, NHS trust web estates, university and local-authority sites, and reverse-proxy tiers in front of Java and PHP applications, and HTTP/2 has been on by default in most distribution builds for years. Two caveats sharpen the risk rather than soften it. First, exploitation status is disputed: one outlet reports Red Hat stating that a reliable exploit has been demonstrated against a default Apache configuration with HTTP/2 enabled, while other trackers record no verified in-the-wild exploitation and no weaponisation as of this window. A containerised differential lab, ThreadSanitizer evidence and a standard-library HTTP/2 proof-of-concept are already published on GitHub under the CVE identifier, so the gap between demonstrated and opportunistic is days, not weeks. Second, the upstream fix does not equal a patched estate: secondary reporting indicates Debian bookworm, trixie and forky had no fixed package at the time of writing and Amazon Linux fixes were pending, while RHEL 9 and 10 shipped. UK organisations that patch only from distribution repositories may have nothing to install yet, which makes the configuration workaround the operative control today. Apache's own advisory lists no workaround; Wiz advises administrators who cannot update to strip h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving 'Protocols http/1.1'. Not KEV-listed as at this window. Detail is from search-result summaries only; httpd.apache.org and the vendor advisory were not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: Inventory every Apache HTTP Server instance and determine which have HTTP/2 enabled - grep the Protocols directive across all vhosts and included config fragments for h2 or h2c; instances without HTTP/2 are not affected and should be de-prioritised.

Upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 (or mod_h2 2.0.43+) where a package exists; on Debian and Amazon Linux, where fixes were still pending in this window, track the distribution security tracker daily.

Where you cannot patch today, apply the mitigation now: set 'Protocols http/1.1' and remove h2/h2c, then reload. Accept the HTTP/2 performance loss as a temporary cost and record it as a deviation to be reverted after patching.

Treat internet-facing and DMZ reverse proxies, load-balancer offload tiers and WAF-origin Apache nodes as the first patch wave; these terminate TLS and ALPN-negotiate h2 and are reachable pre-authentication.

Check appliance and container images, not just OS packages: bundled Apache inside vendor appliances, Docker base images and application stacks (XAMPP-style bundles, older Bitnami images) will not be covered by OS patching.

Hunt for post-exploitation rather than for the exploit itself: a heap-corruption RCE in the web server process yields child processes under the httpd/apache2 service account - look for shells, interpreters and network tooling spawned by the web server.
Raise monitoring sensitivity on httpd/apache2 segmentation faults and worker crashes; the race condition will produce crash-loop noise on failed attempts before successful code execution.

kql.name: Shell or interpreter spawned by Apache worker (CVE-2026-119618 post-exploitation)
kql.description: Untested. Primary behavioural detection: successful heap-corruption RCE in mod_http2 executes in the context of the httpd/apache2 worker, so any shell, interpreter or network tool parented by the web server is high-signal. Baseline legitimate CGI first.
kql.query:
let WebServerProcs = dynamic(["httpd", "apache2", "httpd.exe", "apache.exe"]);
let SuspiciousChildren = dynamic(["sh", "bash", "dash", "zsh", "python", "python3", "perl", "ruby", "php", "nc", "ncat", "netcat", "socat", "curl", "wget", "base64", "chmod", "id", "whoami", "uname", "crontab", "systemctl"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebServerProcs)
| where FileName in~ (SuspiciousChildren)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCommandLine = ProcessCommandLine, Account = AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Outbound connection initiated by Apache worker process (reverse shell / tool pull)
kql.description: Untested. A web server should accept inbound connections, not originate outbound ones to arbitrary internet hosts. Excludes RFC1918, CGNAT and loopback. Expect benign hits where Apache proxies upstream - exclude known upstream destinations.
kql.query:
let WebServerProcs = dynamic(["httpd", "apache2", "httpd.exe", "apache.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebServerProcs)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP)) and not(ipv4_is_in_any_range(RemoteIP, dynamic(["100.64.0.0/10", "127.0.0.0/8", "169.254.0.0/16"])))
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc

kql.name: Apache worker segmentation faults and child-process crash clusters
kql.description: Untested. Failed mod_http2 race exploitation typically crashes the worker before it succeeds, so a cluster of segfault/child-exit messages on an HTTP/2-enabled host is an early warning. Requires the Syslog connector and Apache logging to syslog.
kql.query:
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ProcessName has_any ("httpd", "apache2")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("segmentation fault", "caught SIGSEGV", "child pid", "exit signal", "Segmentation fault")
| summarize Crashes = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Crashes >= 3
| order by Crashes desc

kql.name: Apache HTTP Server versions in the vulnerable 2.4.55-2.4.70 band
kql.description: Untested. Exposure inventory. Vulnerable only where HTTP/2 is enabled, which TVM cannot see - treat output as the candidate set to triage against the Protocols directive, not as a confirmed-vulnerable list.
kql.query:
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareVendor has_any ("apache", "apache_software_foundation")
| where SoftwareName has_any ("http_server", "httpd", "apache")
| extend Major = toint(split(SoftwareVersion, ".")[0]), Minor = toint(split(SoftwareVersion, ".")[1]), Patch = toint(split(SoftwareVersion, ".")[2])
| where Major == 2 and Minor == 4 and Patch between (55 .. 70)
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform
| order by DeviceName asc

vulnerabilities.title: Russia-Aligned Turla Deploys 'Cereal' Backdoor Inside Government Microsoft Exchange Servers to Intercept NATO and EU Email - No External C2, Victim's Own Server Is the Control Channel
affected_products: Microsoft Exchange Server (on-premises; OWA, Autodiscover and ActiveSync request paths abused)
IIS request-handling pipeline on Exchange hosts
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government - highest-relevance espionage development in the window. ESET published research (10 November, widely syndicated 11 November) on 'Cereal', a previously undocumented toolset it attributes with high confidence to the Russia-aligned Turla group, found implanted in on-premises Microsoft Exchange servers at government organisations in Romania and Kazakhstan. The reported objective is email collection, with stolen mail in the Romanian case said to target NATO and EU correspondence. The tradecraft, not the victim list, is why this ranks second for a UK government audience. Cereal was observed with NO external command-and-control infrastructure: the compromised Exchange server itself is the control point, and the backdoor listens on request paths that mimic legitimate Exchange services - Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync. Operators reach it by sending crafted requests to the victim's own public mail endpoint, so there is no beacon, no suspicious outbound connection and no attacker domain to block or hunt for. Every detection assumption built around egress monitoring, DNS sinkholing and C2 IoC feeds fails against this design. ESET notes that using a compromised server as the operational hub is rare, practised by only a handful of APT groups, and that Turla has run variations of it before. Two honest gaps: ESET could not determine how initial access was obtained - exploitation of an Exchange vulnerability is a possibility, not a finding - and could not quantify how much mail was taken. Sources also disagree on the timeline, with the toolset variously described as first discovered in November 2025 and as surfacing during an investigation that began on 28 November 2025 at a Kazakh government body. Attribution rests on a component already publicly tied to Turla being found alongside Cereal and on code resembling older Turla malware. For UK readers the exposure is specific and actionable: UK central government, arm's-length bodies, NHS trusts, local authorities and defence suppliers still run hybrid or legacy on-premises Exchange, Turla's declared collection interest is exactly NATO and EU-facing diplomatic and defence correspondence, and the UK is a NATO member whose departments exchange that traffic daily. Detail is from search-result summaries; the ESET WeLiveSecurity report was not retrievable from this environment, so no file hashes or specific URI strings are available.
recommended_actions: Treat every on-premises or hybrid Exchange server as in scope and run a dedicated compromise assessment - this is a hunt, not a patch, because no CVE and no vendor fix are attached to Cereal.

Enumerate all IIS modules, HTTP handlers and global.asax/web.config handler registrations on Exchange hosts and diff them against a known-good build; a passive implant listening on OWA/Autodiscover/ActiveSync paths must be registered somewhere in the request pipeline.

Hunt IIS logs for requests to OWA, Autodiscover and ActiveSync paths that return unusual status codes or response sizes, arrive from a small set of external IPs, carry anomalous User-Agent strings, or use POST where GET is normal.
Do not rely on outbound/C2 detection for this threat. Cereal was observed with no external C2, so egress blocking, DNS sinkholing and threat-feed matching will not fire.

Review Exchange mailbox access for collection tradecraft: new or modified mailbox export requests, ApplicationImpersonation or full-access delegation grants, EWS access from service accounts, and journaling or transport rules forwarding mail.

Enable and centralise Exchange admin audit logging, IIS logging with full query strings, and PowerShell script-block logging on Exchange hosts; retain at least 12 months given the reported dwell from late 2025.
Prioritise departments and suppliers handling NATO, EU, defence or foreign-policy correspondence, matching the campaign's reported collection interest.

Where an on-premises Exchange server is retained only for hybrid attributes or legacy SMTP relay, use this as the trigger to decommission it - it is an internet-facing code-execution surface with a long exploitation history.
Assume credential and secret compromise on any host found implanted: rotate Exchange service accounts, machine accounts, certificates and any Entra ID application credentials used by the server.

kql.name: Anomalous external access to OWA / Autodiscover / ActiveSync paths (Cereal passive implant hunt)
kql.description: Untested. Cereal listens on paths that imitate legitimate Exchange services, so operator traffic hides in normal mail-endpoint noise. This narrows to external client IPs with few distinct URIs but repeated POSTs - operator behaviour rather than client behaviour. Requires the IIS connector on Exchange servers. Expect heavy benign volume; iterate on the thresholds.
kql.query:
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/owa/", "/Autodiscover/", "/Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync", "/ecp/")
| where isnotempty(cIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))
| summarize Requests = count(), Posts = countif(csMethod =~ "POST"), DistinctUris = dcount(csUriStem), Uris = make_set(csUriStem, 15), Agents = make_set(csUserAgent, 10), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), BytesOut = sum(tolong(scBytes)) by cIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| where Posts >= 5 and DistinctUris <= 3
| order by BytesOut desc

kql.name: DLL or managed assembly written into Exchange / IIS directories
kql.description: Untested. A passive implant registered in the IIS pipeline must land on disk. Flags non-Microsoft writes of executable content into Exchange and IIS paths. Suppress known patch and Cumulative Update activity by excluding msiexec/TrustedInstaller/ServiceHub windows.
kql.query:
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(180d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Microsoft\Exchange Server\", @"\inetpub\", @"\Windows\System32\inetsrv\", @"\Exchange Server\V15\FrontEnd\", @"\Exchange Server\V15\ClientAccess\")
| where FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx" or FileName endswith ".config"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "trustedinstaller.exe", "tiworker.exe", "servicehub.host.dotnet.x64.exe", "setup.exe", "umworkerprocess.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.description: Untested. Hands-on-keyboard activity through a web implant surfaces as children of w3wp.exe running the Exchange application pools, or of Exchange service hosts. Classic Exchange post-exploitation detection, still the highest-value single query for this threat.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(180d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe", "umworkerprocess.exe", "microsoft.exchange.servicehost.exe", "edgetransport.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "whoami.exe", "nltest.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "rundll32.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "wmic.exe", "cscript.exe", "wscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "7z.exe", "rar.exe", "makecab.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Child = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, Account = AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

vulnerabilities.title: NCSC Launches Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) Scheme for UK Critical National Infrastructure - Assured Provider Assurance, Assumed-Breach Methodology, MVP Stage
affected_products: UK critical national infrastructure operators and their regulators/oversight bodies
UK government departments and arm's-length bodies
Commercial providers of adversary simulation / red-team services seeking NCSC assurance
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government - primary in-window UK government development, defensive rather than incident. The NCSC launched its Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme, publishing guidance and scheme documents, with coverage dated 12 November 2026 (Infosecurity Magazine, SC Magazine UK, Industrial Cyber; one newsletter gives 11 November, and Mondaq notes the underlying scheme documents were published on 17 September 2026 ahead of this formal launch). The scheme assures suppliers of adversary simulation services so that organisations can identify trusted providers to test how well they prevent, detect and respond to realistic simulated attacks. It is aimed squarely at the most critical UK organisations - CNI operators, UK government sectors and the regulators and oversight bodies that supervise them - and sits alongside the existing Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and Cyber Resilience Audit, giving regulators a consistent evidence base for resilience claims. Three details matter operationally. First, the methodology is explicitly assumed-breach, which the NCSC recommends for organisations with mature security postures and existing strong detection; immature estates will get more value from CAF work and detection engineering before buying a CyAS engagement. Second, assured providers are not permitted to run fixed attacker playbooks: they must apply an adversarial mindset, conduct continuous and tailored reconnaissance, and develop bespoke approaches to agreed objectives. That is a deliberate break from checklist-driven penetration testing and raises the bar on in-house detection and response. Third, this is a Minimum Viable Product release, so the NCSC can test demand and refine methodology before publishing a fuller operating model and provider listings - organisations should not expect a complete assured-provider list yet, and should monitor NCSC updates. Context makes the timing legible: the NCSC's 3 November 'State of the Cyber Nation' review recorded 80 nationally significant incidents and judged AI-enabled ransomware against UK CNI 'highly likely' by 2028, and the Budget allocated GBP 70m for a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (Nerv) Centre within the NCSC. CyAS is the assurance limb of that programme, and it is also the item in this window that CNI security leaders can act on through procurement and planning rather than emergency patching. Detail is from search-result summaries; ncsc.gov.uk was not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: CNI operators and UK government bodies: read the published CyAS guidance and scheme documents, and assess honestly whether your detection and response maturity justifies an assumed-breach engagement now or whether CAF-aligned detection work should come first.

Treat the assumed-breach premise as a planning assumption, not just a test format: validate that you could detect post-compromise activity (lateral movement, credential access, data staging) without relying on perimeter or initial-access alerts.

Where adversary simulation is already procured, review contracts against the CyAS expectations - bespoke, objective-led, continuously reconnoitred engagements rather than fixed playbooks - and plan to move to assured providers as listings are published.
Monitor NCSC updates for the full operating model and the assured-provider list; the MVP stage means both are incomplete and procurement decisions should allow for change.
Align CyAS outputs with existing CAF and Cyber Resilience Audit evidence so that regulators and oversight bodies receive one consistent resilience narrative rather than three.

Use the scheme as the mandate for purple-team follow-through: book the detection-engineering and response-playbook work to consume engagement findings before the engagement starts, since simulation value is realised in remediation.

Supply-chain application: for critical suppliers, consider requiring evidence of adversary-simulation testing and remediation as a contractual control, in step with the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill trajectory.

vulnerabilities.title: UK Public-Sector Code Exposure: 100+ Serious Flaws Across 349 Public Repositories - Planning Inspectorate Credential Revoked in 20 Minutes, Experts Warn Against Simply Going Private (11 November Update)
vulnerabilities.vendor: Multiple UK government departments and public bodies
affected_products: Public GitHub repositories owned by 33 UK public-sector organisations (349 codebases scanned)
Planning Inspectorate - Microsoft Entra ID application credential committed to a public repository
Scottish Government - administrative token reported in client-side JavaScript
NHS England public source-code repositories (access restricted since May over AI-related concerns)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government - carried from the previous run with material in-window developments. The original finding (WIRED, 10 November) was that a researcher scanning 349 codebases across 33 UK public-sector organisations identified more than 100 serious vulnerabilities, with weaknesses in roughly two-thirds of the organisations examined - the figure describes the sample, not a government-wide vulnerability rate. The headline case was a Microsoft Entra ID application credential for the Planning Inspectorate committed to a public GitHub repository, reportedly capable of granting read-write access to all its SharePoint sites, private staff OneDrive accounts and legally sensitive evidence libraries. Three developments landed inside this window and change the handling. First, the Planning Inspectorate's response is now on record: its monitoring detected the researcher's activity, it revoked the credential within about 20 minutes of receiving the report, and it found no evidence of a data breach. That is a creditable response time and it materially lowers the probability of successful third-party abuse of that specific credential, though it does not address the Git history problem. Second, expert commentary published 11 November (IT Security Guru) reframes the risk: public repositories are continuously and automatically scraped by hostile state-nexus groups and initial access brokers, so the operative question is not whether a secret was spotted but whether it was harvested before revocation - and that cannot be proven either way from the outside. Third, the researcher and independent analysts have warned against the reflexive remedy of pulling repositories private without fixing the underlying flaws: clones and forks already taken remain in circulation, and going dark removes external scrutiny while leaving the vulnerability in place. NHS England's May decision to restrict public access to some source-code repositories over AI security concerns is cited as the cautionary precedent. Standing UK government guidance since May already sets a minimum bar before code is published - a named owner, and controls that stop developers committing secrets - so the gap here is enforcement rather than policy. No public evidence exists that UK government data was stolen through any of these exposures. Detail is from search-result summaries; the WIRED original and the ControlPlane disclosure were not retrievable from this environment, and several aggregator sources carrying this story are low quality.
recommended_actions: Run secret scanning across every public repository your organisation owns, including full Git history and all branches, tags and forks - a revoked credential still present in history is still an exposure record, and rewriting history does not retract clones already taken.

Rotate, do not merely revoke: treat any credential that was ever committed to a public repository as compromised, rotate it, and review what it could reach during its entire validity period, not just since discovery.

For Entra ID application credentials specifically, audit sign-in and audit logs for the full exposure window: service-principal sign-ins from unexpected IPs or ASNs, Graph API calls to SharePoint and OneDrive resources, and any consent or permission changes.
Enable push protection and secret scanning at the organisation level in GitHub, with blocking (not advisory) mode for new commits, and require pre-commit secret detection in CI.

Do not make vulnerable repositories private as the primary remedy - fix the flaws first. Clones already taken are unaffected by visibility changes, and privacy removes external reporting without removing the risk.

Audit client-side JavaScript for embedded tokens and keys across public-facing services; the reported Scottish Government admin token in client-side code is a distinct class from Git-committed secrets and needs a separate sweep.

Confirm compliance with the existing UK government minimum bar for publishing code - a named repository owner and technical controls preventing secret commits - and evidence it per repository rather than per organisation.
Where monitoring detected the researcher, verify the same detection would fire for a hostile actor using the same credential quietly - researcher activity is often noisier than real abuse.

vulnerabilities.title: Barracuda ESG Pre-Auth Root Chain (CVE-2026-116606 + CVE-2026-111560): 17 Exploitation Attempts Observed 9-11 November From 15 IPs in 3 Countries - CISA KEV Deadline 13 November (Tomorrow)
affected_products: Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG) - firmware before 9.4.0.030
Barracuda Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, Web Application Firewall, WAF Control Center, Web Security Gateway (CVE-2026-111560 scope)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - cross-cutting, hardest deadline in this window. Carried from the previous run with new exploitation telemetry. CVE-2026-116606 is a pre-authentication authorisation bypass in the Barracuda Email Security Gateway (CVSS 9.3, reportedly in the ESG password-change logic) that permits a global configuration restore; CVE-2026-111560 is a command-injection flaw (CVSS 8.6). Chained, the vendor states they give an attacker full control of an affected gateway - unauthenticated remote root on a device that sits in front of the mail flow and holds mail-routing configuration and credentials. The in-window development is quantitative. Security firm Previdian reports observing 17 exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-116606 between 9 and 11 November, from 15 IP addresses across three countries. That is one vendor's telemetry, not a confirmed compromise count, and neither Barracuda nor CISA has published exploitation detail or appliance-compromise figures - but it moves this from 'KEV-listed' to 'actively and repeatedly targeted during this window'. Barracuda disclosed observed exploitation in an update posted 21:00 on 9 November; CISA added both CVEs to KEV on 10 November with a remediation due date reported as 13 November 2026 - tomorrow - under a three-day requirement. Two version traps remain unresolved: Barracuda's Campus article is reported to say 9.4.0.029 or later while the CVE record and Mandiant describe versions before 9.4.0.030 as affected, so stopping at 9.4.0.029 may leave you exposed and should be confirmed with Barracuda Support; and CVE-2026-111560 extends beyond ESG to Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF, WAF Control Center and Web Security Gateway, which teams patching only the email gateway will miss. UK relevance is direct: Barracuda ESG is widely deployed across UK local government, NHS trusts, schools and mid-market corporates, frequently as an internet-facing appliance with an administrative interface reachable from outside. Given the history of the 2023 ESG campaign, where compromised appliances required physical replacement rather than patching, any appliance that was internet-exposed and unpatched between 2 and 10 November should be treated as potentially compromised and triaged on that basis, not simply patched and closed. Detail is from search-result summaries; cisa.gov and the Barracuda advisory were not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: Patch Barracuda ESG to firmware 9.4.0.030 or later today - the KEV remediation date is 13 November. Confirm with Barracuda Support whether 9.4.0.029 is sufficient, given the documented version discrepancy; default to 9.4.0.030.
Extend patching for CVE-2026-111560 to Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, Web Application Firewall, WAF Control Center and Web Security Gateway - the command-injection flaw is not ESG-only.
Remove the appliance administrative interface from internet reachability immediately; restrict it to a management VLAN or jump host regardless of patch state.

Treat any appliance that was internet-exposed and unpatched between 2 and 10 November as potentially compromised: review the running configuration against a known-good baseline for unauthorised changes, inspect administrative accounts, and engage incident response where exposure or unexplained changes exist.

Review and diff the gateway configuration specifically for evidence of the global configuration restore primitive being used - restored or altered mail routing, new transport destinations, modified LDAP/AD binds, changed admin credentials or added accounts.
Rotate every credential held on or by the appliance: LDAP/Active Directory bind accounts, SMTP relay credentials, API keys, and administrative passwords. A root-level compromise exposes all of them.
Hunt for mail-flow tampering in the period of exposure: unexpected BCC or journaling destinations, forwarding rules applied at the gateway, and anomalous volumes of mail to unfamiliar domains.

Note the 2023 precedent: in that ESG campaign Barracuda ultimately advised appliance replacement over patching for compromised devices. If you find indicators, plan for replacement rather than cleanup.

vulnerabilities.title: KEV Deadlines Bite Today and Tomorrow: 9 November Batch Due 12 November (OpenSSH 'SSHole' Exploitation Accelerating, GPUStack, FreeSWITCH, IBM Aspera Faspex) and Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-118527 Due 13 November
affected_products: OpenSSH before 10.6p2 on Linux using musl libc without PAM (Alpine Linux default configuration)
GPUStack (authentication flaw, CVE-2026-102895)
SignalWire FreeSWITCH (code injection, CVE-2026-116779)
IBM Aspera Faspex (authorisation flaw, CVE-2026-123218) - note container-image remediation gap
Ivanti Connect Secure 25.1.1.2 and prior, 25.1.2.2 and prior, 22.8R2.5 and prior
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - cross-cutting compliance and exposure bundle. Two KEV deadlines fall inside and immediately after this window. The 9 November batch is due TODAY, 12 November: GPUStack CVE-2026-102895 (authentication flaw), SignalWire FreeSWITCH CVE-2026-116779 (code injection), OpenBSD OpenSSH CVE-2026-123158, and IBM Aspera Faspex CVE-2026-123218 (authorisation flaw). The Ivanti Connect Secure chain's remaining deadline, CVE-2026-118527, falls tomorrow, 13 November. The OpenSSH item - dubbed 'SSHole' - is where exploitation is escalating fastest and deserves the attention. GreyNoise recorded the first successful in-the-wild exploitation on 7 November, roughly 40 hours after the fix in OpenSSH 10.6p2 shipped, and logged 16 successful exploitation chains from six source IPs against protected networks. Previdian reports its first exploitation attempt arriving less than nine hours after CVE publication and confirmed root access on an Alpine Linux honeypot, counting 20 attempts from 13 attacker IPs across nine countries. watchTowr tied observed activity to botnet and cryptomining operations on 6 November, and reporting also describes attempts to install a Python-based backdoor. The critical scoping condition keeps this from being universal: the bug affects OpenSSH before 10.6p2 on Linux systems using musl libc WITHOUT PAM - which is Alpine's default - and exploitation requires specific account conditions, with accounts holding valid password hashes not affected. In practice that points at container images and appliance firmware far more than at mainstream Ubuntu, RHEL or Debian hosts: Alpine is the default base for an enormous share of UK public-sector and corporate container estates, and a container image is exactly the asset class that OS patch compliance reporting does not cover. The same pattern applies to IBM Aspera Faspex, where a container-image remediation gap was noted in the previous run, and Aspera Faspex is used for large-file transfer in UK research, healthcare and media organisations. On Ivanti, Volexity attributes a chain of CVE-2026-104935 (authentication bypass) with CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 to actor UTA0576, achieving unauthenticated root on fully patched appliances from 3 October and then stealing credentials and querying Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys - a post-exploitation objective that turns a VPN compromise into domain-wide exposure. Fixes are in 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6; the 13 October release addressed only CVE-2026-104935, so organisations that patched then are not covered. CISA warns that Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool may not detect CVE-2026-104935 exploitation because attacker commands execute in memory, so compromise assessment needs network and memory forensics, not the vendor tool alone. Detail is from search-result summaries; cisa.gov was not retrievable from this environment and sources disagree on some CVSS values, affected versions and the local-versus-remote precondition for CVE-2026-118527.
recommended_actions: OpenSSH: identify every Alpine-based container image and musl-libc host in your estate and rebuild or patch to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or later. Scan image registries, not just running hosts - a vulnerable base image will keep redeploying the flaw.

OpenSSH scoping: confirm the PAM condition before mass action. Systems using musl libc WITHOUT PAM are affected; accounts with valid password hashes are not exploitable. Use this to triage rather than to dismiss.

OpenSSH hunting: treat any successful SSH authentication for an account that should have no working password as an incident, and hunt for cryptominer and Python-backdoor persistence on exposed Alpine hosts given the botnet and mining activity reported.

Ivanti Connect Secure: upgrade to 25.1.1.3 or 22.8R2.6 before the 13 November deadline. If you patched on 13 October you addressed only CVE-2026-104935 and remain exposed to CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527.

Ivanti compromise assessment: do not rely on the Integrity Checker Tool - CISA states it may miss CVE-2026-104935 exploitation because commands run in memory. Use network telemetry, memory capture and credential-abuse hunting instead.

Ivanti blast radius: assume credential theft on any appliance exposed since 3 October. Rotate VPN and service-account credentials, and treat LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys as compromised - rotate LAPS and re-escrow BitLocker keys.
IBM Aspera Faspex: patch CVE-2026-123218 and verify container-image coverage specifically, as the container distribution lags the appliance fix.

GPUStack and FreeSWITCH: inventory these in research, AI/ML and telephony estates - both are commonly deployed outside central IT visibility. FreeSWITCH underpins UK contact-centre and VoIP platforms.

Record and evidence remediation against the KEV dates (12 and 13 November). UK organisations are not bound by BOD 26-04 but regulators and insurers increasingly treat KEV dates as the reasonableness benchmark.

vulnerabilities.title: Exploited Endpoint Zero-Days Still Open: Microsoft Outlook CVE-2026-124194 (NTLMv2 Leak, KEV Due 24 November) and Chrome/Chromium CVE-2026-125350 (libxslt Use-After-Free, Eighth Chrome Zero-Day of 2026)
affected_products: Microsoft Outlook / Microsoft 365 Apps / Office (patched via Office update channels, not Windows Update)
Google Chrome before 157.0.8103.50
Chromium-based browsers including Microsoft Edge (fix shipped)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - cross-cutting endpoint exposure, carried from the previous run and consolidated. Both items remain actively exploited and both are near-universally deployed across UK central government, local authorities, NHS and UK corporates, which is why they stay in the top ten despite no new in-window development. (1) Microsoft Outlook CVE-2026-124194, the single exploited zero-day in the 10 November Patch Tuesday, is a spoofing and information-disclosure flaw: opening or previewing a crafted message file causes Outlook to reach out to an attacker-controlled location and leak the current user's NTLMv2 hash, which can be relayed to internal services or cracked offline. CVSS is only 6.5 and Microsoft assigns no critical rating, but exploited status plus total deployment makes it the highest-practical-priority Office patch. CISA added it to KEV on 10 November with a due date of 24 November 2026 - treat that as the outside limit rather than the target. The deployment trap persists: at least one outlet reports the fix arrives through the Office / Microsoft 365 Apps update channel rather than Windows Update, so estates patching only via WSUS or Windows Update may report compliant while remaining vulnerable. Verify Office build numbers, not OS patch level, and check Click-to-Run and MSI estates separately. This channel detail remains unconfirmed against Microsoft's own advisory. Three further Outlook remote-code-execution flaws rated critical shipped in the same release (CVE-2026-110043, CVE-2026-110068, CVE-2026-111309); none is reported as exploited, and all should go in the same change window. Patch Tuesday CVE totals continue to conflict across outlets (1,092 per Rapid7, 1,093 per Tenable, 1,094 per Splashtop and CSO, 1,235 per BleepingComputer, with 63-64 rated critical), so work from your own vulnerability-management feed rather than any headline number. (2) Google Chrome CVE-2026-125350 is a use-after-free in the XML/libxslt component, reported by an anonymous researcher on 6 November, with Google confirming an exploit exists in the wild and withholding attack detail. It affects Chrome before 157.0.8103.50 and is the eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching the full-year 2025 total. It was KEV-listed on 10 November. Chromium downstreams including Microsoft Edge have shipped fixes. Chrome updates only apply on relaunch, so a patched-but-unrestarted browser remains exploitable - force relaunch rather than relying on the update badge. Detail is from search-result summaries; msrc.microsoft.com and the Chrome releases blog were not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: Patch Outlook / Microsoft 365 Apps via the Office update channel now and confirm remediation by Office build number, not OS patch level. Audit Click-to-Run and MSI estates separately.

Block outbound SMB (TCP/445) and WebDAV from user workstations to the internet at the perimeter - this neutralises the NTLM-leak primitive even where patching lags, and is the single highest-value compensating control.
Enforce SMB signing and Extended Protection for Authentication on domain controllers, LDAP and internal services to defeat NTLM relay of any hash already captured.
Block NetNTLMv1, begin NTLM auditing, and plan Group Policy restriction of outbound NTLM to remote servers.
Disable the Outlook reading and preview pane for untrusted mail and force plain-text rendering where operationally tolerable until patching completes.
Hunt back 90 days for Outlook-initiated SMB or WebDAV connections to external hosts - exploitation predates the patch, so a clean patch state says nothing about prior compromise.
Apply CVE-2026-110043, CVE-2026-110068 and CVE-2026-111309 (critical Outlook RCE) in the same change window as the exploited flaw.

Force a Chrome relaunch to 157.0.8103.50 or later via policy (RelaunchNotification and RelaunchNotificationPeriod) rather than relying on users restarting; an updated binary with a stale running process is still exploitable.
Apply the equivalent Microsoft Edge and other Chromium-downstream updates, and confirm managed-browser fleets report actual running versions.
Treat the Outlook KEV date of 24 November as an outside limit. Both of these are exploited endpoint flaws in universally deployed software; a two-week window is not a target.

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 3

vulnerabilities.title: SAP November 2026 Patch Day: Four CVSS 10.0 Unauthenticated Flaws in the NetWeaver Stack - 'ICM2SHELL' Memory Corruption, Web Dispatcher, Gateway and a SAML2 Signature-Verification Bypass, No Workarounds
affected_products: SAP NetWeaver Application Server ABAP - Internet Communication Manager (ICM)
SAP Web Dispatcher
SAP Gateway
SAP NetWeaver SAML2 Service Provider (Fiori and Web GUI systems using SSO)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - cross-cutting, highest severity scores in the window. SAP's November 2026 Security Patch Day (10 November) fixed four vulnerabilities carrying the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, all in the NetWeaver stack and none requiring authentication. Two are memory-corruption flaws in the Internet Communication Manager, in NetWeaver AS ABAP (CVE-2026-76964, SAP Note 3778530) and in SAP Web Dispatcher (CVE-2026-89126, Note 3778556); Onapsis, which discovered the ICM flaw and named it 'ICM2SHELL', estimates that thousands of SAP systems with ICM-based HTTP interfaces may be reachable over the public internet. A third 10.0 affects SAP Gateway - sources disagree on the identifier, with one listing CVE-2026-89103 and another describing it without a CVE, so verify against SAP's own Patch Day page. The fourth, CVE-2026-120017, is a missing-authentication flaw in the SAML2 service provider: because signatures are not verified, an attacker can log in as another user, including a privileged one. The fix is Note 3849308, and it should be assumed to affect every Fiori or Web GUI system configured for single sign-on. SAP's advisory reportedly lists no workaround for the SAML2 and Gateway flaws, so patching is the only remedy - there is no configuration change to buy time with. A CSRF flaw (CVE-2026-89119) is rated 9.6, and RedRays counts 38 security notes on the day, nine of them HotNews. No exploitation has been reported as at this window, which is why this sits at rank 8 rather than higher - but the combination of CVSS 10.0, unauthenticated reach, internet-exposed ICM interfaces and the absence of workarounds makes it the most consequential patch-only item in this report. UK relevance is substantial and often under-appreciated: SAP underpins finance, HR, payroll and procurement across UK central government departments, NHS shared-service organisations, local authority back offices, utilities and large UK corporates, and ERP estates are routinely on slower patch cycles than endpoints with change windows measured in weeks. The exploitation history of SAP NetWeaver is the argument for urgency: CVE-2025-31324 moved from disclosure to mass webshell deployment quickly enough that Shadowserver still reports compromised NetWeaver instances from it. Detail is from search-result summaries; the SAP Patch Day page and security notes were not retrievable from this environment, and the Gateway CVE identifier and publication date (10 versus 11 November) conflict between sources.
recommended_actions: Apply SAP Notes 3778530 (NetWeaver AS ABAP ICM), 3778556 (Web Dispatcher), 3849308 (SAML2 service provider) and the Gateway note from the November Patch Day as an emergency change - there are no workarounds for the SAML2 and Gateway flaws.
Identify every internet-reachable ICM-based HTTP interface and SAP Web Dispatcher instance first; Onapsis assesses thousands as publicly exposed, and these are the unauthenticated-reachable assets.

Audit every Fiori and SAP Web GUI system configured for SAML2 single sign-on for CVE-2026-120017 - a signature-verification bypass permitting authentication as an arbitrary privileged user defeats MFA and conditional access upstream of SAP.

Where immediate patching is impossible, remove internet reachability from ICM and Web Dispatcher endpoints and place them behind a reverse proxy or VPN, accepting the service impact; this is a reachability control, not a fix.

Review SAP security audit logs and ICM/Web Dispatcher access logs retrospectively for anomalous unauthenticated requests, malformed HTTP, and crashes or restarts of the ICM process consistent with memory-corruption probing.
Hunt for the NetWeaver webshell pattern established by CVE-2025-31324 exploitation - unexpected files under servlet and public web paths, and new JSP or class files in deployment directories.
Verify SAP Gateway access control lists (secinfo/reginfo) independently of the patch; a hardened Gateway limits exploitation value even where a vulnerability exists.
Confirm patch coverage for the 9.6 CSRF flaw (CVE-2026-89119) and the remaining HotNews notes in the same change window - 38 notes were released, nine HotNews.
Validate against SAP's own Patch Day page: the Gateway CVE identifier differs between secondary sources and should not be tracked from this report alone.

kql.name: External access to SAP ICM, Web Dispatcher and Gateway service ports
kql.description: Untested. Exposure and reconnaissance view covering the standard SAP HTTP/HTTPS instance ports (80NN/443NN), Gateway (33NN/48NN) and dispatcher ports. Replace the host list with your SAP estate; any external source reaching these is an exposure finding in its own right.
kql.query:
let SapHosts = dynamic(["REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_SAP_HOST_IPS"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in (SapHosts)
| where DestinationPort between (8000 .. 8099) or DestinationPort between (44300 .. 44399) or DestinationPort between (3300 .. 3399) or DestinationPort between (4800 .. 4899) or DestinationPort in (50000, 50001, 8080, 443)
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize Requests = count(), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 20), Actions = make_set(DeviceAction, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP
| order by Requests desc

kql.name: SAP ICM and Web Dispatcher process crashes or restarts (memory-corruption probing)
kql.description: Untested. ICM2SHELL-class memory corruption generates crashes before it generates reliable execution, so ICM/Web Dispatcher restarts without a matching change record are an early signal. Requires SAP host syslog forwarding.
kql.query:
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessName has_any ("icman", "sapwebdisp", "disp+work", "gwrd", "sapstartsrv")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("signal 11", "SIGSEGV", "core dump", "process terminated", "restart", "abnormal end", "ICM shutdown", "segmentation")
| summarize Events = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Events >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc

kql.name: Webshell or unexpected deployable written into SAP web and servlet directories
kql.description: Untested. Mirrors the post-exploitation pattern established by CVE-2025-31324 NetWeaver exploitation. Flags web-executable content written into SAP deployment paths by anything other than the SAP deployment tooling.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\usr\sap\", "/usr/sap/", "servlet_jsp", "irj/root", "j2ee/cluster", "sap/public")
| where FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".jspx" or FileName endswith ".class" or FileName endswith ".war" or FileName endswith ".sh" or FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sapstartsrv.exe", "sapstartsrv", "jcontrol.exe", "jcontrol", "sapcpe.exe", "sapcpe", "tp.exe", "r3trans.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.description: Untested. Successful ICM memory-corruption exploitation yields execution in the SAP work-process context. Flags shells and tooling parented by SAP binaries - should be near-zero outside maintenance windows.
kql.query:
let SapProcs = dynamic(["disp+work.exe", "disp+work", "icman.exe", "icman", "sapwebdisp.exe", "sapwebdisp", "gwrd.exe", "gwrd", "jlaunch.exe", "jlaunch"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (SapProcs)
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "sh", "bash", "python", "python3", "perl", "curl", "curl.exe", "wget", "certutil.exe", "nc", "ncat", "whoami.exe", "whoami", "net.exe")

vulnerabilities.summary: UK corporate and UK supply chain - the principal confirmed corporate incident in the window plus the UK leak-site picture. On 11 November, A.P. Moller-Maersk confirmed that an intruder accessed and extracted data from a local legacy system inherited through an acquisition, said the incident appears isolated, and stated that its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. It declined to name the system, the data types or the intrusion date, and reported no impact on other Maersk systems or on customers and partners connected via API or EDI. Separately, a relatively new extortion group calling itself WhiteArmor listed Maersk on its leak site and demanded USD 5m in Bitcoin, claiming roughly 100GB taken from a platform associated with LF Logistics - the Hong Kong company Maersk acquired in 2022 - and specifying around 29,000 driver records, 16,123 staff accounts and over 27,000 mobile device logs. Those figures come solely from the group and are unverified; Maersk has not confirmed WhiteArmor's involvement or the data types, and specialists cited by Danish outlet Ingenioren read this as data theft and extortion rather than conventional encrypting ransomware. The UK relevance is twofold. First, supply chain: Maersk is a primary container carrier for UK import and export flows through Felixstowe, London Gateway and Southampton, and UK logistics, retail and manufacturing firms exchange shipment, customs and driver data with it - so UK organisations should ask whether their own data sat in the acquired LF Logistics estate, not merely whether Maersk is 'affected'. Second, actor continuity: WhiteArmor also claimed UK-headquartered Unilever on 4-5 November, so the same group has now named two UK-linked multinationals in just over a week, suggesting a campaign against large enterprises with complex acquisition histories rather than isolated opportunism. The broader pattern here is the real lesson: the confirmed breach was in a legacy system inherited through acquisition - precisely the asset class that falls outside both the acquirer's standard controls and its asset inventory. UK leak-site activity inside and adjacent to the window comprises Audio Note UK Ltd (claimed by Osiris on 11 November, with a threat to publish unless negotiations open), A&O Shearman (a UK-headquartered international law firm, listed 10-11 November, attributed by one feed to 'BusinessDataLeaks'), Signworx (GB, claimed by Play on 10 November) and Simply UK (7 November). All four are unverified leak-site claims with no victim statement found, and should be treated as investigative leads only - leak-site listings routinely include stale, duplicated and occasionally fabricated victims. Detail is from search-result summaries; BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and Infosecurity Magazine were not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: UK organisations with Maersk or LF Logistics relationships: ask Maersk directly, in writing, whether your data resided in the affected legacy system, rather than relying on the public statement that the incident is 'isolated'.

Treat shipment, customs, driver and personnel data shared with logistics partners as potentially exposed and plan for the downstream consequence - driver and staff records enable convincing phishing and identity-fraud targeting of named individuals.

Run the acquisition-inventory test on your own estate: list every system inherited through merger or acquisition in the last five years, identify which have never been through your standard security baseline, patch cycle, logging onboarding or access review, and schedule assessment in that order. This is the specific failure mode confirmed here.

Brief fraud, finance and HR functions that WhiteArmor has now named two UK-linked multinationals in just over a week, and that extortion groups commonly follow a listing with direct pressure on named employees and customers.

For Audio Note UK, A&O Shearman, Signworx and Simply UK: if you are one of these organisations or a supplier or customer of one, initiate verification now rather than waiting for publication - the extortion window is where notification obligations and legal options are decided.

Where you are a law-firm client (A&O Shearman listing), review what privileged and commercially sensitive material that firm holds, and raise it through your existing supplier-incident process; legal-sector compromise has disproportionate confidentiality consequences.

Do not treat leak-site listings as confirmed breaches in reporting lines to boards or regulators. Record them as unverified claims with a verification owner and a date, and update the record when evidence arrives.

Review outbound data flows to third-party logistics and legal platforms for excess scope - the Maersk case shows that acquired platforms accumulate data that no current contract would justify collecting.

vulnerabilities.title: Check Point Links Three China-Nexus Espionage Clusters Through Shared 'Sparrow' Malware Framework and a Suspected Quartermaster, 'CopperDragon' - European Telecoms, Government, Military and CNI Targeted
vulnerabilities.vendor: Multiple (telecommunications, government, military, research and critical infrastructure targets)
affected_products: Telecommunications operators and transit networks (Europe, Asia, Latin America)
Government and military entities
Research institutions and critical infrastructure operators
Exposed Linux servers and internet-facing RDP (OceanGate access vectors)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - strategic espionage context, in-window research publication. Check Point Research published findings on 11 November from a year-long investigation linking three China-nexus intrusion clusters - tracked as SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire - through a shared malware ecosystem it calls 'Sparrow', and attributing that shared toolkit to a suspected common supplier it names 'CopperDragon'. Check Point describes CopperDragon as a probable 'digital quartermaster' developing tooling for multiple China-nexus actors including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, Tropic Trooper, UAT-9244 and UAT-8302, and assesses some degree of overlap with Salt Typhoon. The campaigns are reported to have targeted several dozen high-profile organisations across three continents: telecommunications operators, government bodies, military entities, research institutions and critical infrastructure in Europe, Asia and Latin America. Access methods differ by cluster, which is the most actionable part of the research - SilentDelivery relies on watering holes and phishing, OceanGate targets exposed Linux servers and RDP password guessing, and DarkWire focuses on telecom and government networks. One Sparrow component is reported to hide command-and-control behind a live legitimate service, a pattern that defeats domain-reputation blocking. Check Point is explicit that shared tooling does not establish a single operator: the report does not claim one team ran all three campaigns, and it does not identify who runs CopperDragon. The '21 countries' figure appears in Check Point's blog summary rather than its technical report and should be treated as approximate. This ranks tenth because it is strategic rather than immediately actionable, but it is directly relevant to UK readers on three counts. Telecommunications and transit networks carrying UK data are named targets, and Salt Typhoon-adjacent activity against telecoms has been a sustained concern for UK and allied agencies. The NCSC's 3 November 'State of the Cyber Nation' review assessed that China highly likely has both the intent and the best positioning to use AI against critical national infrastructure and strategic targets, and this research is a concrete instance of the industrialised tooling that assessment describes. And the quartermaster model has a defensive implication worth internalising: shared tooling across unrelated operators means that indicator-based attribution will mislead, so detection should be anchored on behaviour and tradecraft rather than on actor-labelled IoC feeds. Detail is from search-result summaries; the Check Point Research blog and technical report were not retrievable from this environment, so no hashes, domains or IPs are available here.
recommended_actions: UK telecommunications operators, government bodies and CNI entities: obtain the full Check Point Research report directly and run its indicators against at least 12 months of retained telemetry - the investigation spans a year and dwell times in this class of intrusion are long.

Harden the stated access vectors rather than hunting the malware first: eliminate internet-exposed RDP or place it behind MFA-enforced brokers, and audit internet-facing Linux servers for exposed management services and weak or reused credentials.

Review watering-hole exposure: for sector bodies, regulators and membership organisations whose sites your staff visit routinely, treat a compromise of those sites as a plausible delivery route and ensure browser isolation or hardened configurations for high-risk roles.

Assume indicator-based attribution will be unreliable given shared tooling across unrelated operators. Prioritise behavioural detections - credential access, directory reconnaissance, lateral movement, long-lived low-volume egress - over actor-labelled IoC feeds.

Hunt for command-and-control concealed inside legitimate live services: look for low-volume, long-duration, regularly timed connections to otherwise reputable cloud and content services from servers that have no business reason to use them.

Telecoms specifically: review access to subscriber data, lawful-intercept infrastructure, signalling and routing platforms, and OSS/BSS systems - the collection targets in comparable campaigns against carriers.
Include third-party and managed-service access in scope. Several of the named actor sets historically reached targets through suppliers and shared infrastructure rather than directly.

Feed this into board-level reporting alongside the NCSC's assessment that China highly likely has the intent and positioning to act against UK CNI and strategic targets - it is corroborating evidence for that judgement, not a separate concern.

kql.name: Long-lived low-volume beaconing to legitimate cloud and content services from server workloads
kql.description: Untested. Targets the reported tradecraft of hiding C2 behind a live legitimate service, which defeats domain reputation. Looks for regular, low-volume, many-day connections from servers to reputable services. Expect benign hits from telemetry and update agents - allow-list those processes explicitly, then investigate the remainder.
kql.query:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe", "chrome.exe", "firefox.exe", "onedrive.exe", "teams.exe", "outlook.exe", "msteams.exe", "mssense.exe", "senseir.exe", "omsagent", "mdatp", "waagent")
| summarize Connections = count(), ActiveDays = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1d)), Hours = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1h)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where ActiveDays >= 14 and Connections < 2000 and Hours >= 20
| extend AvgPerDay = round(todouble(Connections) / ActiveDays, 1)
| order by ActiveDays desc

kql.name: RDP password-guessing followed by success (OceanGate access vector)
kql.description: Untested. Directly targets the reported OceanGate vector. Correlates clusters of 4625 failures with a subsequent 4624 type-10 success from the same source. Any pairing from an external IP is an incident.
kql.query:
let Failures =
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
    | where EventID == 4625 and LogonType in (3, 10)
    | summarize FailedAttempts = count(), AccountsTried = dcount(TargetUserName) by IpAddress, Computer, Window = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
    | where FailedAttempts >= 20 or AccountsTried >= 5;
let Successes =
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
    | where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 10
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, IpAddress, Computer, TargetUserName, Window = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h);
Failures
| join kind=inner Successes on IpAddress, Computer, Window
| project Window, IpAddress, Computer, CompromisedAccount = TargetUserName, FailedAttempts, AccountsTried, SuccessTime
| order by FailedAttempts desc

kql.name: Directory and network reconnaissance burst on a single host
kql.description: Untested. Behaviour-first detection as recommended for shared-tooling threats: an operator orientating in a new environment runs several distinct discovery commands in a short window, which a legitimate administrator rarely does. Tune the distinct-tool threshold to your estate.
kql.query:
let Recon = dynamic(["nltest.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "whoami.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "arp.exe", "route.exe", "netstat.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "tasklist.exe", "quser.exe", "qwinsta.exe", "dsquery.exe", "nslookup.exe", "adfind.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FileName in~ (Recon)
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(FileName), Tools = make_set(FileName, 20), Commands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 25), Executions = count() by DeviceName, AccountName, Window = bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where DistinctTools >= 5
| order by DistinctTools desc
